ABSTRACT 
22 
Objectives: To test whether “Nutrition Info” front-of-package food labels proposed by the US 
23 
Food and Drug Administration (FDA) increase purchase healthfulness compared to other 
24 
existing or proposed food labeling systems.  
25 
Methods: We conducted a randomized trial in October-November 2024 (n=5,636 US adults). 
26 
We assessed the effects of 6 front-of-package labeling systems (positive labels only [the status 
27 
quo for many packaged foods]; Nutrition Info labels; positive + Nutrition Info labels; high-in 
28 
labels; positive + high-in labels; and spectrum labels) on healthfulness of purchases from an 
29 
online grocery store. 
30 
Results: Neither the Nutrition Info, positive + Nutrition Info, high-in, nor positive + high-in labels 
31 
led participants to make healthier purchases compared to the positive labels only (range of 
32 
differences:-.04–.54 on a 0-100 healthfulness scale, ps≥.16). The spectrum labels led 
33 
participants to make healthier purchases compared to both the positive labels only 
34 
(difference=2.42, p<.001) and all other labeling systems (range of differences: 1.87–2.45, 
35 
ps<.001) (~3-4% increases).  
36 
Conclusions: Spectrum labels that rate foods from least to most healthy may be more 
37 
promising for promoting healthier purchases than FDA’s proposed Nutrition Info labels. 
38 

 
3
INTRODUCTION 
39 
Poor diet quality is responsible for approximately 500,000 deaths1 and more than $50 
40 
billion in healthcare costs in the US every year.2 While the causes of poor diet quality are 
41 
complex, one important barrier to improving diet quality is that consumers often lack access to 
42 
easy-to-understand nutrition information when deciding what foods to eat. The US requires most 
43 
packaged foods to display the Nutrition Facts Label, but this label is displayed on the back or 
44 
side of product packaging and includes only numerical information that most consumers have 
45 
difficulty understanding.3,4 Experts and policymakers have called for the US to require food 
46 
labels that appear on the front of product packaging and that interpret product healthfulness for 
47 
consumers, rather than only providing numerical information.5,6 Many manufacturers and 
48 
grocery chains have voluntarily implemented these interpretative front-of-package food labels. 
49 
However, voluntary labeling systems typically communicate only about positive attributes,7 
50 
despite evidence that labels which also communicate negative attributes are more effective.7–9  
51 
To address these limitations, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued a 
52 
proposed rule in January 2025 to require an interpretative front-of-package food labeling system 
53 
that would describe negative as well as positive attributes.10 Specifically, FDA proposed 
54 
requiring a “Nutrition Info” label that indicates whether foods contain low, medium, or high levels 
55 
of saturated fat, sodium, and added sugar content (i.e., “nutrients of concern”) as well as the 
56 
percent Daily Value of these nutrients contained in one serving of the product. Almost no 
57 
studies have evaluated these Nutrition Info labels. While the FDA has initially proposed 
58 
requiring Nutrition Info labels, the agency also tested11 and could require “high-in” front-of-
59 
package labels that signal when foods contain excessive levels of nutrients of concern (used in 
60 
Latin America12), or could consider other designs, such as “spectrum” labels that rate overall 
61 
healthfulness (used in Australia13 and France14). It remains unknown, however, whether these 
62 
other new labels outperform positive labels (the status quo for front-of-package labeling for 
63 
many products in the US) or Nutrition Info labels.  
64 

 
4
To address these gaps and inform policymaking, this study aimed to evaluate whether 
65 
the Nutrition Info label and other new front-of-package labels (e.g., high-in labels, spectrum 
66 
labels) lead to healthier purchases compared to positive labels and compared to one another. 
67 
Additionally, because FDA has emphasized that food labels should be designed so that they are 
68 
especially helpful for people with lower nutrition literacy and social privilege,10 we evaluated 
69 
whether the effects of different labels on healthfulness vary by nutrition literacy, income, and 
70 
educational attainment.  
71 
 
72 
METHODS 
73 
Participants 
74 
From October–November 2024, we recruited a sample of US adults through the survey 
75 
research firm CloudResearch Connect. Participants were eligible if they lived in the US, were 
76 
aged 18 years or older, could read and speak English, and were their households’ primary 
77 
shopper (i.e., did >50% of their households’ grocery shopping). The [BLINDED] Institutional 
78 
Review Board approved this study. Prior to data collection, we pre-registered the study on 
79 
ClinicalTrials.gov [BLINDED].  
80 
Setting 
81 
 
The trial took place in a naturalistic online grocery store (eFigure 1 shows an example 
82 
page). Briefly, we created the online store to mirror the look, feel, and functionalities of the e-
83 
commerce site used by Hannaford Supermarkets, a large regional supermarket chain in the US. 
84 
The store included 5,315 products alongside their images, names, and prices as scraped from 
85 
the chain’s website in September 2023. Online stores like this one are realistic, acceptable, and 
86 
valid settings for nutrition research studies.15  
87 
Procedures 
88 
 
Participants completed an online randomized trial. After providing electronic informed 
89 
consent, participants were randomized by Qualtrics software using a simple allocation ratio to 1 
90 

 
5
of 6 trial arms representing different labeling systems: 1) positive, 2) Nutrition Info, 3) high-in, 4) 
91 
positive + Nutrition Info, 5) positive + high-in, or 6) spectrum. We chose to evaluate positive 
92 
labels because they represent the status quo for voluntary food labels in the US, so they offer a 
93 
useful reference point against which to measure new labels. We evaluated Nutrition Info labels 
94 
given the FDA’s interest in these labels.10 We evaluated high-in labels (which signal when foods 
95 
exceed acceptable thresholds for nutrients of concern) and spectrum labels (which provide an 
96 
overall rating of product healthfulness) because other countries have adopted these labels12 and 
97 
because they may improve the healthfulness of food and beverage purchases.16,17 Finally, we 
98 
evaluated the combination of positive + Nutrition Info and positive + high-in labels because if 
99 
FDA’s proposed labels are adopted, Nutrition Info and high-in labels would likely appear 
100 
alongside existing voluntary positive labels. Because positive labels are already commonly 
101 
used, we considered the positive labels the reference group and the other 5 trial arms the 
102 
“intervention” labels. 
103 
Figure 1 shows example labels and eTable 1 details criteria for assigning labels to 
104 
products. The positive arm displayed Guiding Stars labels, among the most widely used positive 
105 
labels in the US.18,19 The positive arm displayed the positive labels on products that met Guiding 
106 
Stars’ criteria for earning 1 (“Good”), 2 (“Better”), or 3 (“Best”) Guiding Stars.20 The Nutrition Info 
107 
arm displayed Nutrition Info labels on all products. Like the FDA’s proposed design,10 the 
108 
Nutrition Info labels we tested indicated whether the product contained low (<5% Daily Value 
109 
[DV]), medium (≥5 to <20% DV), or high (≥20% DV) levels of saturated fat, sodium, and added 
110 
sugar.10,11,21 Unlike the FDA’s proposed labels, however, our Nutrition Info labels omitted %DV 
111 
information and used traffic light color-coding to depict nutrient content levels (green for low, 
112 
yellow for medium, and red for high). Color-coding might trigger automatic associations that help 
113 
consumers interpret product healthfulness.7 The high-in arm displayed high-in labels when the 
114 
product contained ≥20% of the DV per serving of saturated fat, sodium, or added sugar;21 the 
115 
labels mimicked designs that FDA tested prior to the release of their proposed rule.11 The 
116 

 
6
positive + Nutrition Info and positive + high-in arms displayed the Guiding Stars labels alongside 
117 
the Nutrition Info and high-in labels, respectively. The spectrum arm displayed modified Guiding 
118 
Stars labels on all products that ranged from least healthy (“Poor,” 1 star, red labels) to most 
119 
healthy (“Best”, 5 stars, green labels), similar to other spectrum labels.13,14  
120 
Participants completed a shopping task in the online store. Participants were instructed 
121 
to shop as they usually would for items in the following categories: non-alcoholic beverages, 
122 
boxed and frozen meals, breads and baked goods, cereals, snacks, and soups (eTable 2). We 
123 
selected these categories because they are top contributors to intake of nutrients of concern in 
124 
the US,22–27 offer a variety of more and less healthy products, and include almost exclusively 
125 
packaged items that would receive front-of package labels under the FDA’s proposed rule. 
126 
Participants were instructed they had a budget of $35, approximately the median amount spent 
127 
per transaction on these categories at the supermarket chain upon which our store was 
128 
designed. To check out of the online store, participants needed to spend 0.5–1.5 times this 
129 
budget ($17.50–$52.50). Participants were informed that 1 in 50 would be randomly chosen to 
130 
receive their selections delivered to their home and the remainder of their budget as a gift card; 
131 
this procedure incentivized participants to select products they wished to receive. At the end of 
132 
the study, participants were debriefed that those chosen to receive groceries would instead 
133 
receive an electronic gift card for $35. 
134 
After completing the shopping task, participants responded to an online survey. They 
135 
received an incentive from CloudResearch for completing the study.  
136 
Measures 
137 
 
The primary outcome was the healthfulness of participants’ selections in the shopping 
138 
task. We assessed healthfulness using the United Kingdom’s Ofcom Nutrient Profiling Model 
139 
scores,28 which are associated with cardiovascular disease.29 We calculated Ofcom scores for 
140 
all products in the store, converting scores to a 0-100 scale such that higher scores indicate 
141 
healthier selections.28 We calculated average Ofcom scores across all participants’ selections in 
142 

 
7
the shopping task, weighted by the number of servings in each product selected so that Ofcom 
143 
scores better reflected expected consumption of these products. 
144 
 
Secondary nutrition and selection outcomes included overall healthfulness as assessed 
145 
by the average Guiding Stars score of participants’ selections,20 the number of items selected 
146 
that were high in ≥1 nutrient of concern, nutrient densities (e.g., calorie density, sodium density), 
147 
total nutrient amounts (e.g., total calories, total sodium), total number of items selected, and 
148 
total spending in USD.  
149 
 
Secondary psychological outcomes were assessed using survey items. These included 
150 
constructs that may explain how front-of-package labels exert their effects on behavior (e.g., 
151 
thinking about health, negative emotions);30,31 FDA measured in their research (e.g., consumer 
152 
understanding, trustworthiness);32 and may be of interest to policymakers (i.e., public support).  
153 
 
Finally, the survey assessed demographic characteristics and nutrition literacy (using 4 
154 
items from the Newest Vital Sign33). eTable 3 shows survey measures and response options. 
155 
Statistical Analysis  
156 
 
First, we examined the effects of the front-of-package labels on the primary outcome of 
157 
healthfulness (i.e., Ofcom score) using ordinary least squares (OLS) regression. We regressed 
158 
healthfulness on indicator variables for each trial arm, excluding the positive labels arm as the 
159 
referent. We used the model to evaluate whether the intervention labels led to healthier 
160 
purchases than the positive labels, estimating average differential effects (ADEs, i.e., 
161 
differences in predicted means between groups) for each arm compared to the positive labels. 
162 
We also used the model to test whether the five intervention labels (besides the positive labels) 
163 
differed from one another in their effects on healthfulness.  
164 
Second, we examined whether the effects of the labels on healthfulness were 
165 
moderated by nutrition literacy, income, or educational attainment by adding the moderator and 
166 
interactions between the moderator and the trial arms to the primary model. We tested the joint 
167 
significance of the interaction terms and calculated the effect of each arm at each level of the 
168 

 
8
moderator. Third, we examined the effects of the labels on the secondary selection and 
169 
psychological outcomes using a similar approach as for the primary outcome (with OLS 
170 
regression for continuous outcomes, logistic regression for binary outcomes, Poisson regression 
171 
for count outcomes, and mixed effects logistic regression for repeated measures binary 
172 
outcomes).  
173 
We estimated sample size needs to detect a difference in healthfulness between each 
174 
intervention label and the positive labels of Cohen’s d=.15 or larger (based on prior studies8,9,17). 
175 
Assuming a two-tailed critical alpha of 0.05, the target sample size of 5,610 (935 per arm) 
176 
yielded 90% power to detect an effect of this size or larger.  
177 
 
178 
RESULTS 
179 
 
We randomized 6,002 participants; of these, 5,636 participants were included in the 
180 
analyses (Figure 2, all exclusions were pre-registered; most were due to participants not 
181 
completing the shopping task and therefore not providing outcome data). The average age of 
182 
participants was 40.3 years (SD=12.6); 60% identified as female; 76% identified as White, 11% 
183 
as Black, and 6% as Asian or Pacific Islander; 10% identified as Latino (Table 1). Compared to 
184 
the US overall, the sample included somewhat fewer older adults, males, people who identified 
185 
as another race or multi-racial, people with less than a college degree, and people with 
186 
household income ≥$75,000 (eTable 4).  
187 
 
Participants exposed to the positive labels selected groceries with overall healthfulness 
188 
of 58.5 on the 0–100 Ofcom scale (Figure 3, eTable 5). The Nutrition Info labels did not 
189 
improve healthfulness compared to the positive labels (ADE=-.04, 95%CI: -.80, .72; p=.92) 
190 
(Table 2). Similarly, neither the high-in (ADE= .36, 95%CI: -.40, 1.11; p=.36), positive + Nutrition 
191 
Info (ADE= .44, 95%CI: -.32, 1.20; p=.26), nor the positive + high-in (ADE= .54, 95%CI: -.22, 
192 
1.30; p=.16) labels improved healthfulness compared to the positive labels. By contrast, the 
193 
spectrum labels improved healthfulness by approximately 4% compared to the positive labels 
194 

 
9
(ADE=2.42, 95%CI: 1.66, 3.17; p<.001). The effects of the labels on overall healthfulness were 
195 
not moderated by nutrition literacy, income, or educational attainment (ps for interaction≥.29, 
196 
eTable 6).  
197 
When comparing the labels to one another, the spectrum labels were more modestly 
198 
effective at improving healthfulness than the Nutrition Info, high-in, positive + Nutrition Info, and 
199 
positive + high-in labels (approximate improvements of ~3–4%; all ps<.001, Figure 3, eTable 7). 
200 
There were no other differences in overall healthfulness between the labels (ps≥.14).  
201 
In addition to leading to healthier selections as assessed by Ofcom scores, the spectrum 
202 
labels also outperformed the positive labels for most secondary nutrition outcomes (Table 2, 
203 
eTable 8). Specifically, the spectrum labels led to selections with healthier Guiding Stars 
204 
scores, higher fiber density, more total fiber, fewer items that were high in ≥1 nutrient of 
205 
concern, lower calorie density, less total sugar, lower saturated fat density, lower sodium 
206 
density, and less total sodium compared to the reference (positive labels). By contrast, the other 
207 
intervention labels generally did not improve these outcomes compared to the positive labels. 
208 
There were a few exceptions to this pattern. First, the positive + Nutrition Info labels led to 
209 
selections with lower calorie density and lower total sugar compared to the positive labels. 
210 
Second, the high-in and positive + high-in labels led to selections with fewer items high in ≥1 
211 
nutrient of concern. None of the intervention labels led to differences in the total number of 
212 
items selected or total spending in the shopping task compared to the positive labels.  
213 
The intervention labels generally outperformed the positive labels on psychological 
214 
outcomes. For example, each of the intervention labels led to higher likelihood that participants 
215 
correctly identified healthier products (range of ADEs: 5 to 19 percentage points; all ps<.001, 
216 
eTable 9). Likewise, compared to the positive labels, the intervention labels generally led to 
217 
higher likelihood of noticing and using the labels, more thinking about health, more negative 
218 
emotions, and stronger perceptions that the labels were helpful, trustworthy, and 
219 

 
10
understandable. The high-in and positive + high-in labels garnered more public support than the 
220 
positive labels, while the Nutrition Info, positive + Nutrition Info, and spectrum labels did not.  
221 
 
222 
DISCUSSION 
223 
In this randomized trial in a large sample of US adults, ‘spectrum’ food labels that rated 
224 
all foods from least to most healthy led participants to select modestly healthier foods and 
225 
beverages compared to the status quo of displaying only positive labels on healthier foods. 
226 
Spectrum labels also led to healthier selections compared to other designs for new labels, 
227 
including the Nutrition Info and high-in labels studied or proposed by FDA. The effects of the 
228 
food labels on healthfulness did not vary by nutrition literacy, income, or education. Together, 
229 
these results suggest that adopting spectrum labels could improve diet quality without 
230 
exacerbating health disparities.  
231 
The spectrum labels led to overall healthier selections compared to all other labeling 
232 
systems we tested. One possible explanation for why the spectrum labels outperformed the 
233 
positive and high-in labels is that the spectrum labels were applied to all products, rather than 
234 
only to healthier or less healthy products. The Nutrition Info labels were also displayed on all 
235 
products, but the spectrum labels may have outperformed those labels because they provided a 
236 
single summary interpretation of product healthfulness (e.g., “Fair,” “Best”), while the Nutrition 
237 
Info labels required consumers to integrate potentially conflicting information about three 
238 
different nutrients. Our results align with prior studies finding that spectrum labels improve the 
239 
healthfulness of food and beverage purchases17 and suggest that adopting spectrum labels 
240 
could modestly improve diet quality.  
241 
In this study, Nutrition Info labels similar to FDA’s proposed labels did not lead to 
242 
healthier selections than positive labels, regardless of whether they were presented alone or 
243 
alongside positive labels. The Nutrition Info labels we studied used traffic-light color coding to 
244 
convey when foods were low (green), medium (yellow), or high (red) in nutrients of concern, 
245 

 
11
while the FDA’s proposed Nutrition Info label is black and white. Traffic-light color coding could 
246 
elicit automatic associations that amplify label effectiveness;7 thus, our Nutrition Info labels may 
247 
be even stronger than FDA’s proposed labels. Together, these results suggest that the currently 
248 
proposed Nutrition Info labels may not maximize the public health benefits of new front-of-
249 
package labels.  
250 
In conducting research to inform its proposed rule, FDA also studied high-in labels 
251 
similar to those we tested.11 In our study, high-in labels (whether presented alone or alongside 
252 
positive labels) did not lead to healthier selections than positive labels, suggesting that the high-
253 
in labels as designed by FDA (i.e., depicted on a single white, square-shaped label) also may 
254 
not improve the healthfulness of food and beverage purchases. Our findings stand in contrast to 
255 
robust evidence that high-in labels as designed by many Latin American countries (i.e., depicted 
256 
on multiple black, octagon-shaped labels) lead to meaningful improvements in the healthfulness 
257 
of food and beverage purchases.9,16 Together with prior research, our results suggest that if 
258 
FDA pursues a high-in label, designs more similar to labels in Latin America may be more 
259 
effective.  
260 
In the U.S., the First Amendment limits how and when the government can compel 
261 
companies to display mandatory labels on their products,34 and industry sometimes challenges 
262 
labeling policies on these grounds. In hearing these challenges, courts consider whether the 
263 
content of mandatory labels is “purely factual, accurate, and uncontroversial.”34 FDA’s Nutrition 
264 
Info labels include interpretative information (i.e., whether foods are low, medium, or high in 
265 
nutrients of concern) that is clearly linked to established regulatory definitions of these terms, 
266 
which may strengthen arguments that these labels are factual and uncontroversial. By contrast, 
267 
the spectrum labels we tested are not tied to current federal regulations, which could make it 
268 
more difficult for these labels to clear First Amendment challenges. Future research should 
269 
explore how to design spectrum labels such that they are linked to federal regulations, such as 
270 
federal guidelines for nutrient content or the FDA’s definition of “healthy.” Likewise, although the 
271 

 
12
high-in labels used in Latin American countries have shown considerable promise for improving 
272 
public health, the octagonal shape of these labels could be deemed controversial,34 and FDA 
273 
might consider other shapes (e.g., rectangles) if they pursue Latin-American-style high-in labels.  
274 
FDA has emphasized that a core objective of mandating front-of-package food labels is 
275 
to help consumers identify healthier foods. In our study, the Nutrition Info, high-in, and spectrum 
276 
labels all increased the likelihood that participants correctly identified healthier foods compared 
277 
to the status quo of positive labels. Adopting new front-of-package labels–regardless of design–
278 
could therefore support FDA’s goal of promoting consumer understanding.   
279 
Strengths of this study include the large and diverse sample, the randomized design, 
280 
and the use of a realistic online grocery store. Limitations include that participants had a single 
281 
exposure to the labels in the context of an online store; effects after repeated exposures and in 
282 
brick-and-mortar settings remain unknown. Second, we recruited a convenience sample that 
283 
differed in some respects from the US overall, limiting generalizability. However, randomized 
284 
trials conducted with convenience samples generally replicate in probability samples.35 Third, 
285 
although we incentivized participants to select groceries they wished to receive, participants did 
286 
not pay for or receive their selections.  
287 
 
288 
CONCLUSIONS 
289 
In this randomized trial, spectrum food labels that rated foods from least to most healthy 
290 
led participants to select healthier foods and beverages compared to positive, Nutrition Info, and 
291 
high-in labels. Spectrum labels may be more promising than both existing positive labels and 
292 
the FDA’s proposed Nutrition Info labels for promoting healthier purchases.

Title: Testing FDA’s proposed “Nutrition Info” label against other front-of-package food labels: A 
1 
randomized trial 
2 
 
3 
Authors: Anna H. Grummon,1,2 Kevin O’Sullivan,3 Joshua Petimar,4 Cristina J.Y. Lee,1 Amanda 
4 
B. Zeitlin,1 Lauren P. Cleveland,5 Caroline Collis,5 Aviva A. Musicus,6, 7 Verena Tiefenbeck,8

13

Medical School, Boston, MA, USA

21

2
ABSTRACT 
22 
Objectives: To test whether “Nutrition Info” front-of-package food labels proposed by the US 
23 
Food and Drug Administration (FDA) increase purchase healthfulness compared to other 
24 
existing or proposed food labeling systems.  
25 
Methods: We conducted a randomized trial in October-November 2024 (n=5,636 US adults). 
26 
We assessed the effects of 6 front-of-package labeling systems (positive labels only [the status 
27 
quo for many packaged foods]; Nutrition Info labels; positive + Nutrition Info labels; high-in 
28 
labels; positive + high-in labels; and spectrum labels) on healthfulness of purchases from an 
29 
online grocery store. 
30 
Results: Neither the Nutrition Info, positive + Nutrition Info, high-in, nor positive + high-in labels 
31 
led participants to make healthier purchases compared to the positive labels only (range of 
32 
differences:-.04–.54 on a 0-100 healthfulness scale, ps≥.16). The spectrum labels led 
33 
participants to make healthier purchases compared to both the positive labels only 
34 
(difference=2.42, p<.001) and all other labeling systems (range of differences: 1.87–2.45, 
35 
ps<.001) (~3-4% increases).  
36 
Conclusions: Spectrum labels that rate foods from least to most healthy may be more 
37 
promising for promoting healthier purchases than FDA’s proposed Nutrition Info labels. 
38

3
INTRODUCTION 
39 
Poor diet quality is responsible for approximately 500,000 deaths1 and more than $50 
40 
billion in healthcare costs in the US every year.2 While the causes of poor diet quality are 
41 
complex, one important barrier to improving diet quality is that consumers often lack access to 
42 
easy-to-understand nutrition information when deciding what foods to eat. The US requires most 
43 
packaged foods to display the Nutrition Facts Label, but this label is displayed on the back or 
44 
side of product packaging and includes only numerical information that most consumers have 
45 
difficulty understanding.3,4 Experts and policymakers have called for the US to require food 
46 
labels that appear on the front of product packaging and that interpret product healthfulness for 
47 
consumers, rather than only providing numerical information.5,6 Many manufacturers and 
48 
grocery chains have voluntarily implemented these interpretative front-of-package food labels. 
49 
However, voluntary labeling systems typically communicate only about positive attributes,7 
50 
despite evidence that labels which also communicate negative attributes are more effective.7–9  
51 
To address these limitations, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued a 
52 
proposed rule in January 2025 to require an interpretative front-of-package food labeling system 
53 
that would describe negative as well as positive attributes.10 Specifically, FDA proposed 
54 
requiring a “Nutrition Info” label that indicates whether foods contain low, medium, or high levels 
55 
of saturated fat, sodium, and added sugar content (i.e., “nutrients of concern”) as well as the 
56 
percent Daily Value of these nutrients contained in one serving of the product. Almost no 
57 
studies have evaluated these Nutrition Info labels. While the FDA has initially proposed 
58 
requiring Nutrition Info labels, the agency also tested11 and could require “high-in” front-of-
59 
package labels that signal when foods contain excessive levels of nutrients of concern (used in 
60 
Latin America12), or could consider other designs, such as “spectrum” labels that rate overall 
61 
healthfulness (used in Australia13 and France14). It remains unknown, however, whether these 
62 
other new labels outperform positive labels (the status quo for front-of-package labeling for 
63 
many products in the US) or Nutrition Info labels.  
64

4
To address these gaps and inform policymaking, this study aimed to evaluate whether 
65 
the Nutrition Info label and other new front-of-package labels (e.g., high-in labels, spectrum 
66 
labels) lead to healthier purchases compared to positive labels and compared to one another. 
67 
Additionally, because FDA has emphasized that food labels should be designed so that they are 
68 
especially helpful for people with lower nutrition literacy and social privilege,10 we evaluated 
69 
whether the effects of different labels on healthfulness vary by nutrition literacy, income, and 
70 
educational attainment.  
71 
 
72 
METHODS 
73 
Participants 
74 
From October–November 2024, we recruited a sample of US adults through the survey 
75 
research firm CloudResearch Connect. Participants were eligible if they lived in the US, were 
76 
aged 18 years or older, could read and speak English, and were their households’ primary 
77 
shopper (i.e., did >50% of their households’ grocery shopping). The [BLINDED] Institutional 
78 
Review Board approved this study. Prior to data collection, we pre-registered the study on 
79 
ClinicalTrials.gov [BLINDED].  
80 
Setting 
81 
 
The trial took place in a naturalistic online grocery store (eFigure 1 shows an example 
82 
page). Briefly, we created the online store to mirror the look, feel, and functionalities of the e-
83 
commerce site used by Hannaford Supermarkets, a large regional supermarket chain in the US. 
84 
The store included 5,315 products alongside their images, names, and prices as scraped from 
85 
the chain’s website in September 2023. Online stores like this one are realistic, acceptable, and 
86 
valid settings for nutrition research studies.15  
87 
Procedures 
88 
 
Participants completed an online randomized trial. After providing electronic informed 
89 
consent, participants were randomized by Qualtrics software using a simple allocation ratio to 1 
90

5
of 6 trial arms representing different labeling systems: 1) positive, 2) Nutrition Info, 3) high-in, 4) 
91 
positive + Nutrition Info, 5) positive + high-in, or 6) spectrum. We chose to evaluate positive 
92 
labels because they represent the status quo for voluntary food labels in the US, so they offer a 
93 
useful reference point against which to measure new labels. We evaluated Nutrition Info labels 
94 
given the FDA’s interest in these labels.10 We evaluated high-in labels (which signal when foods 
95 
exceed acceptable thresholds for nutrients of concern) and spectrum labels (which provide an 
96 
overall rating of product healthfulness) because other countries have adopted these labels12 and 
97 
because they may improve the healthfulness of food and beverage purchases.16,17 Finally, we 
98 
evaluated the combination of positive + Nutrition Info and positive + high-in labels because if 
99 
FDA’s proposed labels are adopted, Nutrition Info and high-in labels would likely appear 
100 
alongside existing voluntary positive labels. Because positive labels are already commonly 
101 
used, we considered the positive labels the reference group and the other 5 trial arms the 
102 
“intervention” labels. 
103 
Figure 1 shows example labels and eTable 1 details criteria for assigning labels to 
104 
products. The positive arm displayed Guiding Stars labels, among the most widely used positive 
105 
labels in the US.18,19 The positive arm displayed the positive labels on products that met Guiding 
106 
Stars’ criteria for earning 1 (“Good”), 2 (“Better”), or 3 (“Best”) Guiding Stars.20 The Nutrition Info 
107 
arm displayed Nutrition Info labels on all products. Like the FDA’s proposed design,10 the 
108 
Nutrition Info labels we tested indicated whether the product contained low (<5% Daily Value 
109 
[DV]), medium (≥5 to <20% DV), or high (≥20% DV) levels of saturated fat, sodium, and added 
110 
sugar.10,11,21 Unlike the FDA’s proposed labels, however, our Nutrition Info labels omitted %DV 
111 
information and used traffic light color-coding to depict nutrient content levels (green for low, 
112 
yellow for medium, and red for high). Color-coding might trigger automatic associations that help 
113 
consumers interpret product healthfulness.7 The high-in arm displayed high-in labels when the 
114 
product contained ≥20% of the DV per serving of saturated fat, sodium, or added sugar;21 the 
115 
labels mimicked designs that FDA tested prior to the release of their proposed rule.11 The 
116

6
positive + Nutrition Info and positive + high-in arms displayed the Guiding Stars labels alongside 
117 
the Nutrition Info and high-in labels, respectively. The spectrum arm displayed modified Guiding 
118 
Stars labels on all products that ranged from least healthy (“Poor,” 1 star, red labels) to most 
119 
healthy (“Best”, 5 stars, green labels), similar to other spectrum labels.13,14  
120 
Participants completed a shopping task in the online store. Participants were instructed 
121 
to shop as they usually would for items in the following categories: non-alcoholic beverages, 
122 
boxed and frozen meals, breads and baked goods, cereals, snacks, and soups (eTable 2). We 
123 
selected these categories because they are top contributors to intake of nutrients of concern in 
124 
the US,22–27 offer a variety of more and less healthy products, and include almost exclusively 
125 
packaged items that would receive front-of package labels under the FDA’s proposed rule. 
126 
Participants were instructed they had a budget of $35, approximately the median amount spent 
127 
per transaction on these categories at the supermarket chain upon which our store was 
128 
designed. To check out of the online store, participants needed to spend 0.5–1.5 times this 
129 
budget ($17.50–$52.50). Participants were informed that 1 in 50 would be randomly chosen to 
130 
receive their selections delivered to their home and the remainder of their budget as a gift card; 
131 
this procedure incentivized participants to select products they wished to receive. At the end of 
132 
the study, participants were debriefed that those chosen to receive groceries would instead 
133 
receive an electronic gift card for $35. 
134 
After completing the shopping task, participants responded to an online survey. They 
135 
received an incentive from CloudResearch for completing the study.  
136 
Measures 
137 
 
The primary outcome was the healthfulness of participants’ selections in the shopping 
138 
task. We assessed healthfulness using the United Kingdom’s Ofcom Nutrient Profiling Model 
139 
scores,28 which are associated with cardiovascular disease.29 We calculated Ofcom scores for 
140 
all products in the store, converting scores to a 0-100 scale such that higher scores indicate 
141 
healthier selections.28 We calculated average Ofcom scores across all participants’ selections in 
142

7
the shopping task, weighted by the number of servings in each product selected so that Ofcom 
143 
scores better reflected expected consumption of these products. 
144 
 
Secondary nutrition and selection outcomes included overall healthfulness as assessed 
145 
by the average Guiding Stars score of participants’ selections,20 the number of items selected 
146 
that were high in ≥1 nutrient of concern, nutrient densities (e.g., calorie density, sodium density), 
147 
total nutrient amounts (e.g., total calories, total sodium), total number of items selected, and 
148 
total spending in USD.  
149 
 
Secondary psychological outcomes were assessed using survey items. These included 
150 
constructs that may explain how front-of-package labels exert their effects on behavior (e.g., 
151 
thinking about health, negative emotions);30,31 FDA measured in their research (e.g., consumer 
152 
understanding, trustworthiness);32 and may be of interest to policymakers (i.e., public support).  
153 
 
Finally, the survey assessed demographic characteristics and nutrition literacy (using 4 
154 
items from the Newest Vital Sign33). eTable 3 shows survey measures and response options. 
155 
Statistical Analysis  
156 
 
First, we examined the effects of the front-of-package labels on the primary outcome of 
157 
healthfulness (i.e., Ofcom score) using ordinary least squares (OLS) regression. We regressed 
158 
healthfulness on indicator variables for each trial arm, excluding the positive labels arm as the 
159 
referent. We used the model to evaluate whether the intervention labels led to healthier 
160 
purchases than the positive labels, estimating average differential effects (ADEs, i.e., 
161 
differences in predicted means between groups) for each arm compared to the positive labels. 
162 
We also used the model to test whether the five intervention labels (besides the positive labels) 
163 
differed from one another in their effects on healthfulness.  
164 
Second, we examined whether the effects of the labels on healthfulness were 
165 
moderated by nutrition literacy, income, or educational attainment by adding the moderator and 
166 
interactions between the moderator and the trial arms to the primary model. We tested the joint 
167 
significance of the interaction terms and calculated the effect of each arm at each level of the 
168

8
moderator. Third, we examined the effects of the labels on the secondary selection and 
169 
psychological outcomes using a similar approach as for the primary outcome (with OLS 
170 
regression for continuous outcomes, logistic regression for binary outcomes, Poisson regression 
171 
for count outcomes, and mixed effects logistic regression for repeated measures binary 
172 
outcomes).  
173 
We estimated sample size needs to detect a difference in healthfulness between each 
174 
intervention label and the positive labels of Cohen’s d=.15 or larger (based on prior studies8,9,17). 
175 
Assuming a two-tailed critical alpha of 0.05, the target sample size of 5,610 (935 per arm) 
176 
yielded 90% power to detect an effect of this size or larger.  
177 
 
178 
RESULTS 
179 
 
We randomized 6,002 participants; of these, 5,636 participants were included in the 
180 
analyses (Figure 2, all exclusions were pre-registered; most were due to participants not 
181 
completing the shopping task and therefore not providing outcome data). The average age of 
182 
participants was 40.3 years (SD=12.6); 60% identified as female; 76% identified as White, 11% 
183 
as Black, and 6% as Asian or Pacific Islander; 10% identified as Latino (Table 1). Compared to 
184 
the US overall, the sample included somewhat fewer older adults, males, people who identified 
185 
as another race or multi-racial, people with less than a college degree, and people with 
186 
household income ≥$75,000 (eTable 4).  
187 
 
Participants exposed to the positive labels selected groceries with overall healthfulness 
188 
of 58.5 on the 0–100 Ofcom scale (Figure 3, eTable 5). The Nutrition Info labels did not 
189 
improve healthfulness compared to the positive labels (ADE=-.04, 95%CI: -.80, .72; p=.92) 
190 
(Table 2). Similarly, neither the high-in (ADE= .36, 95%CI: -.40, 1.11; p=.36), positive + Nutrition 
191 
Info (ADE= .44, 95%CI: -.32, 1.20; p=.26), nor the positive + high-in (ADE= .54, 95%CI: -.22, 
192 
1.30; p=.16) labels improved healthfulness compared to the positive labels. By contrast, the 
193 
spectrum labels improved healthfulness by approximately 4% compared to the positive labels 
194

9
(ADE=2.42, 95%CI: 1.66, 3.17; p<.001). The effects of the labels on overall healthfulness were 
195 
not moderated by nutrition literacy, income, or educational attainment (ps for interaction≥.29, 
196 
eTable 6).  
197 
When comparing the labels to one another, the spectrum labels were more modestly 
198 
effective at improving healthfulness than the Nutrition Info, high-in, positive + Nutrition Info, and 
199 
positive + high-in labels (approximate improvements of ~3–4%; all ps<.001, Figure 3, eTable 7). 
200 
There were no other differences in overall healthfulness between the labels (ps≥.14).  
201 
In addition to leading to healthier selections as assessed by Ofcom scores, the spectrum 
202 
labels also outperformed the positive labels for most secondary nutrition outcomes (Table 2, 
203 
eTable 8). Specifically, the spectrum labels led to selections with healthier Guiding Stars 
204 
scores, higher fiber density, more total fiber, fewer items that were high in ≥1 nutrient of 
205 
concern, lower calorie density, less total sugar, lower saturated fat density, lower sodium 
206 
density, and less total sodium compared to the reference (positive labels). By contrast, the other 
207 
intervention labels generally did not improve these outcomes compared to the positive labels. 
208 
There were a few exceptions to this pattern. First, the positive + Nutrition Info labels led to 
209 
selections with lower calorie density and lower total sugar compared to the positive labels. 
210 
Second, the high-in and positive + high-in labels led to selections with fewer items high in ≥1 
211 
nutrient of concern. None of the intervention labels led to differences in the total number of 
212 
items selected or total spending in the shopping task compared to the positive labels.  
213 
The intervention labels generally outperformed the positive labels on psychological 
214 
outcomes. For example, each of the intervention labels led to higher likelihood that participants 
215 
correctly identified healthier products (range of ADEs: 5 to 19 percentage points; all ps<.001, 
216 
eTable 9). Likewise, compared to the positive labels, the intervention labels generally led to 
217 
higher likelihood of noticing and using the labels, more thinking about health, more negative 
218 
emotions, and stronger perceptions that the labels were helpful, trustworthy, and 
219

10
understandable. The high-in and positive + high-in labels garnered more public support than the 
220 
positive labels, while the Nutrition Info, positive + Nutrition Info, and spectrum labels did not.  
221 
 
222 
DISCUSSION 
223 
In this randomized trial in a large sample of US adults, ‘spectrum’ food labels that rated 
224 
all foods from least to most healthy led participants to select modestly healthier foods and 
225 
beverages compared to the status quo of displaying only positive labels on healthier foods. 
226 
Spectrum labels also led to healthier selections compared to other designs for new labels, 
227 
including the Nutrition Info and high-in labels studied or proposed by FDA. The effects of the 
228 
food labels on healthfulness did not vary by nutrition literacy, income, or education. Together, 
229 
these results suggest that adopting spectrum labels could improve diet quality without 
230 
exacerbating health disparities.  
231 
The spectrum labels led to overall healthier selections compared to all other labeling 
232 
systems we tested. One possible explanation for why the spectrum labels outperformed the 
233 
positive and high-in labels is that the spectrum labels were applied to all products, rather than 
234 
only to healthier or less healthy products. The Nutrition Info labels were also displayed on all 
235 
products, but the spectrum labels may have outperformed those labels because they provided a 
236 
single summary interpretation of product healthfulness (e.g., “Fair,” “Best”), while the Nutrition 
237 
Info labels required consumers to integrate potentially conflicting information about three 
238 
different nutrients. Our results align with prior studies finding that spectrum labels improve the 
239 
healthfulness of food and beverage purchases17 and suggest that adopting spectrum labels 
240 
could modestly improve diet quality.  
241 
In this study, Nutrition Info labels similar to FDA’s proposed labels did not lead to 
242 
healthier selections than positive labels, regardless of whether they were presented alone or 
243 
alongside positive labels. The Nutrition Info labels we studied used traffic-light color coding to 
244 
convey when foods were low (green), medium (yellow), or high (red) in nutrients of concern, 
245

11
while the FDA’s proposed Nutrition Info label is black and white. Traffic-light color coding could 
246 
elicit automatic associations that amplify label effectiveness;7 thus, our Nutrition Info labels may 
247 
be even stronger than FDA’s proposed labels. Together, these results suggest that the currently 
248 
proposed Nutrition Info labels may not maximize the public health benefits of new front-of-
249 
package labels.  
250 
In conducting research to inform its proposed rule, FDA also studied high-in labels 
251 
similar to those we tested.11 In our study, high-in labels (whether presented alone or alongside 
252 
positive labels) did not lead to healthier selections than positive labels, suggesting that the high-
253 
in labels as designed by FDA (i.e., depicted on a single white, square-shaped label) also may 
254 
not improve the healthfulness of food and beverage purchases. Our findings stand in contrast to 
255 
robust evidence that high-in labels as designed by many Latin American countries (i.e., depicted 
256 
on multiple black, octagon-shaped labels) lead to meaningful improvements in the healthfulness 
257 
of food and beverage purchases.9,16 Together with prior research, our results suggest that if 
258 
FDA pursues a high-in label, designs more similar to labels in Latin America may be more 
259 
effective.  
260 
In the U.S., the First Amendment limits how and when the government can compel 
261 
companies to display mandatory labels on their products,34 and industry sometimes challenges 
262 
labeling policies on these grounds. In hearing these challenges, courts consider whether the 
263 
content of mandatory labels is “purely factual, accurate, and uncontroversial.”34 FDA’s Nutrition 
264 
Info labels include interpretative information (i.e., whether foods are low, medium, or high in 
265 
nutrients of concern) that is clearly linked to established regulatory definitions of these terms, 
266 
which may strengthen arguments that these labels are factual and uncontroversial. By contrast, 
267 
the spectrum labels we tested are not tied to current federal regulations, which could make it 
268 
more difficult for these labels to clear First Amendment challenges. Future research should 
269 
explore how to design spectrum labels such that they are linked to federal regulations, such as 
270 
federal guidelines for nutrient content or the FDA’s definition of “healthy.” Likewise, although the 
271

12
high-in labels used in Latin American countries have shown considerable promise for improving 
272 
public health, the octagonal shape of these labels could be deemed controversial,34 and FDA 
273 
might consider other shapes (e.g., rectangles) if they pursue Latin-American-style high-in labels.  
274 
FDA has emphasized that a core objective of mandating front-of-package food labels is 
275 
to help consumers identify healthier foods. In our study, the Nutrition Info, high-in, and spectrum 
276 
labels all increased the likelihood that participants correctly identified healthier foods compared 
277 
to the status quo of positive labels. Adopting new front-of-package labels–regardless of design–
278 
could therefore support FDA’s goal of promoting consumer understanding.   
279 
Strengths of this study include the large and diverse sample, the randomized design, 
280 
and the use of a realistic online grocery store. Limitations include that participants had a single 
281 
exposure to the labels in the context of an online store; effects after repeated exposures and in 
282 
brick-and-mortar settings remain unknown. Second, we recruited a convenience sample that 
283 
differed in some respects from the US overall, limiting generalizability. However, randomized 
284 
trials conducted with convenience samples generally replicate in probability samples.35 Third, 
285 
although we incentivized participants to select groceries they wished to receive, participants did 
286 
not pay for or receive their selections.  
287 
 
288 
CONCLUSIONS 
289 
In this randomized trial, spectrum food labels that rated foods from least to most healthy 
290 
led participants to select healthier foods and beverages compared to positive, Nutrition Info, and 
291 
high-in labels. Spectrum labels may be more promising than both existing positive labels and 
292 
the FDA’s proposed Nutrition Info labels for promoting healthier purchases.
